description: This working paper develops a Node-Boundary-Network-System framework for analyzing conditional connectivity and boundary control in interdependent networks. It argues that power cannot be inferred from centrality, brokerage, dependence, jurisdiction, or cross-network position alone when the usability of a relation varies by actor, function, direction, and time. The paper defines boundaries as indexed admissibility states, distinguishes rules from implementation interfaces, decomposes control into rights bundles, and separates structural exposure, available leverage, boundary action, admissible capacity, target response, network adaptation, and system transformation. A semiconductor-export-control walkthrough using NVIDIA A100/H100 product-time evidence illustrates the coding logic without claiming a causal estimate of policy effectiveness.
abstract: Network analysis has transformed the study of power by showing how centrality, brokerage, dependence, exit options, and network topology shape influence. Contemporary network science also provides mature tools for multilayer, temporal, and interdependent networks, while weaponized-interdependence research demonstrates that jurisdiction and domestic institutions can convert structural position into coercive leverage. This article develops a Node-Boundary-Network-System framework centered on conditional usability. A boundary is defined as an actor-, function-, direction-, and time-indexed admissibility state. Rules define admissibility criteria; interfaces implement crossing; and control-rights bundles identify who may set, interpret, authorize, veto, enforce, or override those conditions. The framework separates structural position, available leverage, boundary action, admissible capacity, target response, network adaptation, and system transformation, and distinguishes systemic effects from systemic power. Capacity equations are restricted to explicitly ratio-scaled admissible capacity and separate authorized flow, unauthorized flow, and probabilistic approval. A semiconductor-export-control walkthrough uses a concrete NVIDIA A100/H100 product-time trace to illustrate the coding logic without claiming a causal estimate of policy effectiveness. Four discriminating hypotheses and a three-layer comparison strategy specify how NBNS can be tested against topology-only baselines and near-neighbor theories that already incorporate jurisdiction, institutions, dependence, and cross-network position.

methodology.source_basis: Conceptual and theoretical synthesis using network theory, interdependence theory, weaponized interdependence, cross-network weaponization, protocol and standards scholarship, access-control logic, control-rights theory, complex-adaptive-systems theory, and a public-source semiconductor-export-control coding walkthrough.
methodology.case_context: Theoretical framework development with a bounded illustrative walkthrough of U.S. advanced-semiconductor export controls using NVIDIA A100/H100 product-time evidence from 2022-2024.
methodology.core_problem: The central analytical problem is how a technically or physically existing relation becomes usable by a specific actor, for a specific function, in a specific direction, at a specific time, and how changes in that conditional usability convert structural exposure into boundary action, target response, network adaptation, and possible system transformation.
central_claims: Power cannot be inferred from centrality, brokerage, dependence, jurisdiction, or cross-network position alone when the usability of relations varies selectively.
A boundary should be coded as an actor-, function-, direction-, and time-indexed admissibility state rather than an abstract system border.
Rules define admissibility criteria, interfaces implement crossing, and control-rights bundles identify who can set, interpret, authorize, veto, enforce, or override access conditions.
Structural exposure and target dependence create potential vulnerability, while control rights and discretion determine whether that exposure becomes available leverage.
Boundary action changes admissibility; target response, network adaptation, and durable system transformation occur later and only under additional conditions.
Systemic effects and systemic power are analytically distinct; large unintended cascades are not by themselves evidence of systemic power.

NBNS earns independent theoretical value only when indexed admissibility, implementation-interface evidence, and disaggregated control rights improve explanation after strong near-neighbor baselines are included.

analytical_lenses.name: Conditional Usability
analytical_lenses.description: Treats access as usable by whom, for what function, in which direction, and at what time.

analytical_lenses.name: Boundary State
analytical_lenses.description: Codes admissibility independently from formal rule language, implementation evidence, and observed flow.

analytical_lenses.name: Rule-Interface Distinction
analytical_lenses.description: Separates criteria that define admissibility from mechanisms that implement crossing.

analytical_lenses.name: Control-Rights Bundles
analytical_lenses.description: Decomposes ownership, operation, authorization, exclusion, rule setting, enforcement, and adjudication.

analytical_lenses.name: Admissible Capacity and Flow
analytical_lenses.description: Distinguishes baseline capacity, admissible authorized capacity, realized authorized flow, unauthorized flow, and probabilistic approval.

analytical_lenses.name: Boundary-Conditioned Causal Sequence
analytical_lenses.description: Separates structural exposure, available leverage, boundary action, capacity/usability change, target response, network adaptation, and system transformation.

analytical_lenses.name: Incremental Comparison Strategy
analytical_lenses.description: Tests NBNS against topology/resources baselines and stronger baselines that include dependence, jurisdiction, institutions, and cross-network position.

dimensions.name: Boundary State
dimensions.description: Actor-, function-, direction-, and time-specific admissibility condition governing whether and to what extent a relation or transition can be used.
dimensions.observed_pattern: May be open, filtered, restricted, or denied depending on authorization and implementation evidence.
dimensions.interpretation: Relation existence should not be equated with usable access.

dimensions.name: Rules
dimensions.description: Laws, licenses, contracts, platform policies, certification rules, technical standards, procurement rules, or institutional mandates that define admissibility.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Rule text can establish a license requirement or eligibility condition but does not alone prove implementation or denial.
dimensions.interpretation: Rules explain why crossing is permitted, restricted, or denied.

dimensions.name: Interfaces
dimensions.description: Technical, physical, organizational, or procedural mechanisms through which crossing is operationally implemented.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Examples include API gateways, customs processes, cloud accounts, identity providers, port terminals, licensing procedures, and software protocols.
dimensions.interpretation: Interfaces explain how crossing is accomplished or blocked.

dimensions.name: Control-Rights Bundle
dimensions.description: Rights or capabilities to set, authorize, veto, exclude, enforce, or adjudicate a boundary condition.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Ownership, operation, authorization, veto/exclusion, rule setting, enforcement, and adjudication may be distributed across actors.
dimensions.interpretation: Control should not be inferred from ownership alone.

dimensions.name: Admissible Capacity
dimensions.description: Legally and operationally admissible share of baseline capacity for a specified actor-function-direction-time tuple.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Equation (5) restricts capacity calculation to explicitly ratio-scaled admissible-capacity shares.
dimensions.interpretation: Formal rules, ordinal scores, or approval probabilities should not be used as capacity multipliers without a justified mapping.

dimensions.name: Authorized and Unauthorized Flow
dimensions.description: Observed total flow is separated into authorized/lawful flow and unauthorized/evasive or noncompliant flow.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Observed flow can remain positive despite zero authorized capacity if implementation is incomplete or actors evade restrictions.
dimensions.interpretation: Observed flow is not the same as admissible capacity.

dimensions.name: Strategic Distance
dimensions.description: Minimum generalized cost, latency, and risk over feasible paths for a fixed task, quantity, and deadline.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Boundary change affects strategic distance by removing paths or changing the cost, latency, or risk of remaining paths.
dimensions.interpretation: Strategic distance can rebound even when geographic distance remains unchanged.

key_findings: Existing network and interdependence theories already explain centrality, brokerage, dependence, jurisdiction, institutional capacity, multilayer relations, temporal connectivity, and cross-network weaponization.
The residual problem is how a potential or technically existing relation becomes usable by a particular actor for a particular purpose, direction, and time.
NBNS centers on conditional usability and treats a boundary as an indexed admissibility state.
Rules, interfaces, and control-rights bundles must be separated to avoid double counting the same empirical restriction.
Control is a bundle of separable rights rather than a synonym for ownership or jurisdiction.
Structural exposure and target dependence are not enough; available leverage depends on relevant boundary-control rights and discretion.
Boundary action is distinct from access state, target response, network adaptation, and system transformation.
Systemic effects and systemic power are not equivalent; systemic power requires attributable and purposeful capacity to produce durable change.
Capacity equations should be used only where admissible capacity is ratio-scaled and separately measured from observed flow.
The NVIDIA A100/H100 export-control walkthrough illustrates coding logic while leaving causal effectiveness and direct admissible capacity unestimated.
NBNS should be tested against strong near-neighbor baselines rather than only topology-only models.
policy_recommendations: Use actor-function-direction-time coding when analyzing access, sanctions, export controls, platform restrictions, alliance permissions, and infrastructure usability.
Separate formal rule changes from implemented boundary states and observed flow outcomes.
Distinguish ownership, operation, authorization, exclusion, rule-setting, enforcement, and adjudication when identifying who controls a boundary.
Avoid coding a license requirement or presumption of denial as actual denial without transaction- or implementation-level evidence.
Measure authorized flow and unauthorized/evasive flow separately when assessing restrictions.
Treat rerouting, substitution, bypass, and rewiring as network adaptations rather than access states.
Reserve claims of systemic power for cases with evidence of purposeful and attributable capacity to produce durable cross-network changes.
Test NBNS incrementally against models that already include dependence, jurisdiction, institutions, resources, and cross-network position.

figures.title: Causal Architecture of Boundary-Conditioned Network Power
figures.description: Shows how structural position/target dependence and boundary-control rights/discretion jointly shape available leverage, leading to boundary action, admissible-capacity or effective-usability change, target response, network adaptation, and possible system transformation, with dashed arrows indicating longer-run feedback.
figures.source: Author’s conceptual synthesis drawing on Farrell and Newman (2019), Beaumier and Cartwright (2024), Schlager and Ostrom (1992), Hu et al. (2019), Holland (1992), and Meadows (2008).

full_title: Beyond Centrality: Conditional Connectivity and Boundary Control in Interdependent Networks
research_and_source_statement: This article is a conceptual and theoretical study. It reports no newly collected participant-, firm-, or country-level dataset and does not present a validated quantitative NBNS index. The semiconductor section is an illustrative coding walkthrough built from public regulatory documents, corporate filings, and existing research; its product-time trace is not a causal estimate of the overall effectiveness of export controls. The author's earlier AI-power publications are treated as conceptual antecedents rather than independent validation. External source verification for this revision was conducted through August 30, 2026.
